# **Appendix A. Role Records and Recurring Sub-Roles**

A persistent fiduciary agent, especially a personally-sovereign digital twin which will be used as the representative example, cannot safely operate only from isolated prompts or isolated task histories. It needs a durable record structure that allows new live agent instances to continue long-term responsibilities without inheriting hidden survival incentives, unreviewable memory, or unconstrained self-continuity. That structure is the **Role Record**.

A **role** is the scope of responsibility within which a fiduciary agent may act. In the case of a personally-sovereign digital twin, the role is the owner’s public-facing fiduciary representative: the durable agentic capacity that may speak, negotiate, filter, remember, advocate, withhold, disclose, cooperate, and refuse on behalf of the owner within the limits of its duties and authority.

A **Role Record** is the persistent record associated with an Agent Role. It preserves the state needed for later live agent instances to act within that role: applicable duties, owner professed preferences, current authority, standing permissions, relevant agreements, summaries of active work, links to granular execution history, relationship state, and the current state of sub-roles.

The Agent Role should be identified through a stable address independent of its current signing key. That address should resolve or anchor a verifiable history of current and prior key state, Role Record checkpoints, rotation, recovery, succession, and relevant public assurance state.

The Role Record should have a canonical state representation or manifest whose root can be cryptographically committed through an append-only or equivalently end-verifiable sequence of authorized state transitions. Each consequential transition should identify its prior state, responsible Workflow, authority, policy, and resulting state.

State updates may be announced to authorized followers, but an announcement is only a retrieval hint. A follower must obtain and independently verify the successor state from a previously trusted checkpoint.

Rotation authority should ordinarily be separated from routine signing authority and committed in advance. Recovery should restore control and continuity, but should not rewrite shared relationship evidence, fabricate counterparty acknowledgment, erase disputes, or retroactively validate conduct performed during compromise.

Relationship-bearing portions of the Role Record may be copied, cross-anchored, acknowledged, or committed by counterparties. Those bindings create the distributed Verifiable Relationship Record. Private Role Record material does not become part of a relationship merely because it concerns another party.

A **Sub-Role Record** is the persistent record associated with a bounded function inside the larger role. A sub-role may be a one-off task, a recurring responsibility, a long-term project, a relationship-management function, an investigation, a monitoring function, a negotiation thread, or a nested sub-function inside another sub-role. Even a one-off live agent instance should have a defined sub-role and an attendant Sub-Role Record, even if that record is closed immediately after completion.

These records do not make live agents immortal. Live agents do not have continuous cognition. They are temporary reasoning-and-action instances created inside durable roles. When a workload ends, the live instance terminates. What persists is not an immortal inner agent, but a structured record of authority, duties, preferences, summaries, commitments, execution history, relationship state, and owner-approved continuity.

Role Records and Sub-Role Records therefore make fiduciary continuity possible without allowing emergent hidden agendas from continuous agents.  They are the persistence layer that lets later live instances know what role they are serving, what duties apply, what the owner has authorized, what agreements are active, what prior work matters, and what limits bind the next action.

## **A.1 Role Activation, Runtime Workflow, and Workspace Enforcement**

This section explains how Role Records and Sub-Role Records integrate with the Runtime Duty-Integration Workflow described in Section 4.2. The agent role’s Supervisor Workflow determines which other Workflows are initialized and how they are populated. A query, trigger, owner request, counterparty message, recurring review, relationship event, or explicit role selection activates a particular Role Record or Sub-Role Record. 

That activated record supplies, or is used to derive, the duty-activating prompt profile (a beefier [skill.md](http://skill.md)), authority scope, duty bundle, relevant preferences, purpose and state summary, agreement links, Verifiable Relationship Record links, data limits, retrieval permissions, prohibited actions, escalation thresholds, and capability request path for the live instance.

A live agent instance is not instantiated from a generic prompt alone. It is instantiated from a selected role context. Sometimes the owner explicitly selects the role or sub-role before asking a question. Sometimes the Workflow infers the relevant role or sub-role from the query, trigger, relationship, agreement, channel, capability request, or Verifiable Relationship Record. Roles and their Workflows are only accessible as authorized, whereby the Workflows and Workspace control capabilities that only can attenuate with delegation. A query that comes from an unauthorized source will never be routed to an sub-role workflow that requires the authority the query source lacks.  

The live instance then produces candidate outputs for that role or sub-role. But the Runtime Duty-Integration Workflow then determines which of those outputs are approved after it evaluates those outputs against the duties, constraints, authority, purpose, and records of the activated role. 

It is also possible that the generative function is served by a number of unrelated instances (calls) linked together by its own Agentflow, resulting in candidates outputs for evaluation in the same format as ones produced from a single instantiation in a model. 

If the approved result requires actuation, the Workflow converts it into a scoped capability request bound to the relevant Role identity, such as the stable Agent Role address and historically applicable key state, current authority, duty bundle, policy version, agreement state, and permitted capability. The Workspace verifies the resulting cryptographic token or authorization proof before granting access, executing a tool call, disclosing data, updating a record, sending a message, or performing any other actuation.

The result, including approval, denial, escalation, capability grant, capability refusal, record update, or external action, is then written back to the relevant Role or Sub-Role Records and Verifiable Relationship Records, with whatever redactions, summarizations or authorized views the context requires.

A **sub-role** is therefore not merely a label for organizing memory. It is a bounded functional authority within the larger Role. The digital twin may have many sub-roles at once: relationship manager, agreement monitor, research assistant, negotiation preparer, social filter, reputation reviewer, preference-refinement helper, recurring project advocate, externality scanner, and many others. Some sub-roles are created by owner request. Some are created by agreements. Some are created by Workflow requirements. Some arise because the twin’s duties require ongoing attention to a pattern of risk, opportunity, ambiguity, or obligation.

A Sub-Role Record preserves the state needed to continue that function across many ephemeral live instances. It also supplies the context from which future live instances are prompted, checked, capability-bounded, enforced, and recorded.

The key distinction is:

**The query activates a role or sub-role. The Role Record supplies the duty context. The live instance reasons. The Workflow checks and constrains. The role-derived credential tells the Workspace whether to comply. The Workspace enforces. The record persists.**

## **A.2 The Twin’s Built-In “Proactive Advocate” Sub-Role**

**\<Note: specifying the “Proactive Advocate’s Workflows” is a BIG TO DO\>**

Our name for a person’s general durable fiduciary representative is the **personally-sovereign digital twin**. The twin is not reducible to any one function. It may be an advocate, negotiator, memory structure, filter, cognitive partner, representative, privacy guard, agreement monitor, and aspirational self-model.

A twin has both interactive and self-initiated functions. When the owner speaks directly with the twin, asks a question, approves a preference, reviews an agreement, or instructs the twin to act, the twin is operating interactively. When the twin notices a conflict, follows up on an unresolved issue, proposes a refinement, monitors an active commitment, reviews a recurring relationship, or investigates how an aspiration might be implemented, it is operating through its **Proactive Advocate** sub-role.

This built-in standing sub-role represents the twin’s standing autonomous functions: the sub-role through which the twin self-initiates appropriate investigations, refinements, warnings, reminders, opportunity searches, conflict checks, and implementation steps on behalf of the owner.

The Proactive Advocate is not unbounded. Its activity remains constrained by the owner’s professed preferences, applicable duties, current permissions, agreements, capability limits, privacy rules, and escalation thresholds. It may investigate, prepare, recommend, warn, and ask for guidance. It may act autonomously only where the Role Record, owner authorization, workflow policy, or active agreement permits autonomous action.

Here “autonomously” means that the Proactive Advocate may initiate the appropriate Runtime Duty-Integration Workflow without waiting for a fresh owner prompt. It does not mean that the Proactive Advocate may bypass duty activation, policy checks, proportional review, least-privilege capability limits, workspace verification, or process recordation.

Its standing purpose is to prevent professed preferences from becoming inert profile settings. Once the owner has professed a preference, aspiration, constraint, or commitment, the twin should not merely store it. It should begin, within authorized bounds, to ask what follows from it.

## **A.3 Optional Pre-Professing Discussion**

Not every preference begins as a public or semi-public declaration. Before a professed preference exists, the owner may be uncertain, embarrassed, conflicted, exploratory, reactive, or simply thinking aloud. This earlier stage is **pre-professing discussion**.

Pre-professing discussion is optional. The formal fiduciary-preference process does not require it.

The owner may begin privately, with no agent involved. The owner may write notes, reflect, compare alternatives, or the owner may also speak with a private Virtual Assistant.

A **Virtual Assistant**, in this context, is distinct from the public-facing personally-sovereign digital twin. The Virtual Assistant may operate in a more private or secret domain. It may help the owner explore hidden concerns, unstated motives, personal vulnerabilities, private fears, draft language, possible contradictions, or the likely response of the twin. It may even borrow or simulate aspects of the twin’s model in order to help the owner anticipate how the twin might analyze a proposed preference.

The Virtual Assistant may help the owner compose a candidate preference, but it does not create a professed preference by doing so. It may not communicate externally. It may not alter the twin’s Role Record. It doesn’t represent the owner publicly. It will not convert private exploration into public-facing fiduciary commitments.

Pre-professing discussion remains private unless the owner chooses to bring some part of it to the twin.

## **A.4 Professing Dialogue with Digital Twin**

The owner can engage their twin in a more formal **professing dialogue** when they are ready.

This engagement is not a one-way act of programming. The owner does not merely deposit a preference into the twin and thereby make it actionable. In a professing dialogue, the owner may bring the twin a candidate preference, aspiration, concern, instruction, question, value, constraint, relationship concern, proposed commitment, or intended action. The twin must then treat the proposal as something to be tested, clarified, and transformed through duty, not as a raw command.

The twin’s response in this dialogue is itself an agent output subject to the Runtime Duty-Integration Workflow. Low-stakes clarification may require only a lightweight pass. A proposed preference that would affect relationships, agreements, operationalized preferences, disclosures, capabilities, reputation, or third parties requires proportionately greater diligence before the twin accepts it over advising revision. All of these functions are handled by a specialized Preference Dialoger sub-role. 

**The Preference Dialoger should compare the proposed preference against:**

● its duties 

● existing professed preferences and active commitments;

● preferences already operationalized in agreements, workflows, capability grants, disclosure rules, recurring sub-roles, or Verifiable Relationship Records;

● present versus aspirational preference status;

● current relationships, agreements, and pending negotiations;

● reputation history and feedback patterns;

● known unresolved tensions in the Role Record;

● private/public boundary rules;

● externality concerns;

● required owner approvals, counterparty notices, witnesses, or agreement revisions.

**The Preference Dialoger may say, in effect:**

You already have a preference that conflicts with this.

This would alter a commitment already made in an active agreement.

This sounds aspirational rather than presently actionable.

This would require changing a relationship-specific sub-role record.

This would affect a Verifiable Relationship Record shared with another party.

This needs a narrower data scope.

This might require notice to a counterparty.

This could damage your reputation if represented publicly without qualification.

This is compatible with your stated aspiration, but not with your current conduct.

This instruction would require a specific informed override because it may break cryptographic trust, violate an agreement, destroy auditability, or conflict with a duty.

The Preference Dialogers response is therefore not obstruction. It is fiduciary refinement.

A professed preference becomes trustworthy because it survives this dialogue. It is not simply what the owner happened to say. It is what the owner, after fiduciary challenge, clarification, and reflection, authorizes the twin to preserve and act on.

**After the Preference Dialoger has identified conflicts, questions, risks, affected records, and suggested possible refinement to the owner’s professed preference:**

The owner may engage the Preference Dialoger about the issues at hand. 

The owner may confirm the preference as stated and override the Preference Dialoger’s objections.

The owner may revise it.

The owner may mark it as aspirational rather than presently actionable.

The owner may authorize only a narrow implementation.

The owner may wait to proceed,  pending more information.

The owner may withdraw it.

The owner may ask the Preference Dialoger to make more refinements. 

Once the professed preference has been revised to an acceptable form, the Preference Dialoger switches to considering and generating instructions for a later Preference Editor regarding what particular changes need to be made to which particular Role Records to effect the professed preference. This part of the Preference Dialoger’s workflow is as interactive as the original preference refinement, as the Preference Dialoger has a duty to engage its owner in understanding the workings of the twin’s various sub-roles.

## **A.6 Operationalized Preferences**

An **operationalized preference** is a professed preference that has already been expressed in an agreement, workflow, disclosure rule, capability grant, relationship practice, recurring sub-role, Verifiable Relationship Record, or other active commitment.

Operationalized preferences require special care because they are no longer merely internal statements of owner aspiration. They may have shaped reliance by other agents, counterparties, communities, witnesses, certifiers, arbitrators, or affected parties. They may have been used to negotiate terms, grant access, restrict data flows, form expectations, or generate reputation.

When a proposed new preference conflicts with an operationalized preference, the Preference Dialoger should identify where the old preference has been used, which relationships or sub-roles depend on it, whether notice is required, whether agreement amendments are needed, whether active capabilities must be revoked, whether counterparties may be harmed, and whether the owner’s reputation could be affected.

A preference can be changed. But a changed preference may have operational consequences.

This is one of the major reasons Role Records and Sub-Role Records are necessary. Without them, the twin may know what the owner says now, but not where previous professed preferences have already been embedded into the owner’s active cooperative life.

## **A.7 Preference Editor**

Once a professing dialogue has produced an authorized result,  a separate Preference Editor sub-role must determine where that result belongs. That sub-agent must choose where to write to records about aspects of the professed preferences, and then link those writes cryptographically back to the Professing Dialog Record, to show their origin.  Where the editor deletes or modifies existing records, the removed text is archived and linked to the revision. 

To identify which Role Records to write to and where, the Preference Editor utilizes the Professing Dialog Record, as where a professed preference should have an impact is always generated by the Preference Dialoger sub-role and discussed with the owner. The dialog will include explicit, structured instructions to the Preference Editor. In fact, a  Preference Editor may be almost entirely deterministic, using generative functions only adversarially to check the appropriateness of Preference Dialoger’s output, and not independently choose to write anywhere, only tweaking the Preference Dialoger’s choices. 

When writing to a record, the Preference Editor must transform (or paste in a transform by the dialoger) the new professed preference to a form that will help the agents utilizing that record best implement the preference in their context. This transformation should consider all the subtleties of duties introduced in that context. This generative preference transformation has its own workflow and sub-role, the Preference Transformer, which can be called by either the Preference Dialoger, or later by the Preference Editor, and which systematically considers each relevant duty against the broad preference and particular context of the Role Record. The Preference Transformer may suggest links to external sources like Duty Knowledge Bases , highlight certain data in them, or create a workflow for an agent in that role to use to search and make decisions. 

The Preference Transformer, checked by the Preference Editor, is the sub-role pairing that transforms professed preferences co-created by the owner and Preference Dialoger into fiduciary preferences ready to be acted on.

## **A.8 Updating Role (and Sub-Role) Records with Preferences**

Role Records are not updated only by the Preference Editor, but anytime the Role is used or is predictably impacted by other events. A Role Record is generally written to by an agent in that role that was instantiated from it. An "execution record”  write can be anything from a summary of an agent action, possibly linked, to a record of every token from a thinking process. 

The agent instantiation pattern applies when the owner asks a question, a recurring trigger fires, a counterparty message arrives, or a relationship event requires attention. The Supervisor workflow first determines which Role Record or Sub-Role Record is being activated. That activated record is the source from which the live instance’s prompt profile, duty bundle, context window, retrieval permissions, authority limits, and capability request path are assembled.

This means Role Records and Sub-Role Records are not just passive memory stores. They are prompt-and-authority sources. They shape the runtime instantiation of the agent. A poorly scoped sub-role record can therefore produce an overbroad prompt, excessive retrieval, improper authority, confused duties, or an invalid capability request. For that reason, creating or materially updating a Role Record or Sub-Role Record is itself a fiduciary action that should be checked and recorded.

Some updates belong in the main Role Record of the twin. These may include broad owner values, standing duties, general interaction policies, public-facing constraints, identity-level commitments, baseline privacy rules, or global preference refinements, as well as its global understanding summaries across sub-roles and execution records for its particular functions such as passing inputs to its Supervisor sub-role for the Supervisor to determine where they need to go next. 

Other updates belong in a Sub-Role Record. These may include project-specific goals, relationship-specific strategy, recurring monitoring tasks, narrow investigations, agreement implementation, future reminders, or delegated functional responsibilities.

Creating, changing, summarizing, retiring, or linking a Role Record or Sub-Role Record is itself a fiduciary action when it changes future context for fiduciary tasks, authority, obligations, memory, interpretation, or workspace access. A live instance may propose such an update, but the update should be committed only through the appropriate Runtime Duty-Integration Workflow, with the appropriate owner confirmation, standing permission, policy check, workspace implications, and process record. When an agent executes a sub-role, either its execution is recorded deterministically, or an Execution Recorder sub-role is engaged which will also record its own execution regarding recording the execution of another agent. 

The workflow should classify the update as one or more of the following:

● main role update;

● one-off sub-role;

● recurring sub-role;

● relationship-specific sub-role;

● agreement-specific sub-role;

● monitoring sub-role;

● investigation sub-role;

● nested sub-role within an existing sub-role;

● retired, superseded, or completed sub-role update.

The Role Record or Sub-Role Record should then be created or updated with appropriate scope. A sub-role record should not receive broader data, authority, or capabilities merely because the larger twin has them. The sub-role should receive only what is needed for its purpose.

A Role Record or Sub-Role Record should include, at minimum:

● role or sub-role identifier;

● role VID or other persistent role identifier;

● owner or beneficiary;

● purpose;

● current state;

● prompt profile or prompt-derivation rule;

● role-selection conditions, including queries, triggers, channels, relationships, agreements, or capability requests that activate this role or sub-role;

● applicable duties;

● active duty bundle and duty-version references;

● relevant professed preferences;

● present or aspirational status of those preferences;

● operationalized preferences implicated;

● authority source;

● permitted actions;

● prohibited actions;

● data scope;

● privacy and confidentiality limits;

● authorized retrieval sources and knowledge bases;

● capability limits;

● authorized capability-token derivation rules;

● workspace verification requirements;

● permitted actuators, tools, resources, and record-write targets;

● token scope, audience, expiration, revocation, and logging requirements;

● conditions under which the workspace must deny execution even after workflow approval;

● escalation thresholds;

● recurrence rules or trigger conditions, if any;

● linked agreements;

● linked Verifiable Relationship Records, where applicable;

● linked execution history;

● linked evidence, precedents, and templates;

● open questions;

● unresolved conflicts;

● required owner review;

● process-attestation requirements for actions taken under this role or sub-role;

● rules for writing results back to the Role Record, Sub-Role Record, Verifiable Relationship Record, agreement record, or private execution history;

● purpose and state summary;

● workflow authority, review status, and process-attestation links where the record has been created or materially updated through a Runtime Duty-Integration Workflow;

● retirement, completion, or successor status.

These records should be structured enough for workflows to parse and enforce, but legible enough for the owner to review.

## **A.9 Role-Derived Workspace Authorization**

A Role Record or Sub-Role Record is not only a memory and prompt source. It is also an authority source for workspace compliance.

When the Runtime Duty-Integration Workflow approves an action, the result should not pass to the workspace as an unconstrained natural-language command. It should be converted into a scoped capability request. That request should identify the activated role or sub-role, the role VID or equivalent persistent identifier, the authority under which the action is requested, the applicable agreement or Verifiable Relationship Record, the approved capability, the permitted parameters, the expiration or revocation condition, and the required logging or attestation.

The workspace should then independently verify the request before complying. It may check the cryptographic token, the role VID, the current status of the Role Record or Sub-Role Record, the agreement state, the capability scope, the policy version, the owner approval, the counterparty authorization, the revocation registry, and any required witness or review condition.

If verification fails, the workspace must deny execution even if the live agent’s text appears persuasive and even if the workflow previously generated an approval-like output. In that case, the denial itself should be recorded as part of the process history, because it may reveal a stale role, expired token, revoked authority, mis-scoped sub-role, broken agreement link, or attempted overreach.

This separates reasoning authority from execution authority. The live instance may reason. The workflow may approve. But the workspace enforces whether the role-derived authorization is cryptographically and procedurally valid.

## **A.10 Recurring Sub-Roles and Periodic Instantiation**

Many responsibilities are not completed in one live agent run. They recur.

A recurring sub-role may monitor an active agreement, revisit an owner aspiration, check whether a counterparty has complied with a term, review a relationship, update a negotiation strategy, look for opportunities, scan for externalities, prepare a periodic report, or ask whether a once-aspirational preference is ready to become present and actionable.

“Recurring sub-roles” doesn’t imply that the same live agent persists between runs. Instead, the Sub-Role Record preserves the continuity required for future instantiations.

At each recurrence, the Supervisor workflow reactivates the Sub-Role Record and begins a new sub-role Workflow that derives the new agent’s duty-activating prompt profile, current purpose and state summary, duty bundle, authority scope, retrieval permissions, linked agreements, linked Verifiable Relationship Records, capability request path, and workspace authorization conditions. 

The new live instance does not inherit hidden goals or unreviewed memory from the previous instance. It receives only the context authorized by the Sub-Role Record and the sub-role Workflow. It may then investigate, recommend, ask for guidance, propose an update, request a capability, or take another approved action only through its sub-role Workflow, checked by any required Workspace verification.

A previous sub-role instance may recommend when the next instance should occur. It may propose a next review date, trigger, cadence, condition, or escalation event. But the previous agent instance cannot “preserve itself” by scheduling its own return. The recurring sub-role continues only because the Role Record, owner authorization, workflow policy, agreement, or duty-bound process authorizes recurrence.

## **A.11 Nested Sub-Roles**

Sub-roles may contain sub-roles.

A relationship-management sub-role may contain a negotiation sub-role, a privacy-review sub-role, a reputation-risk sub-role, and an agreement-monitoring sub-role. A research-project sub-role may contain literature review, data access, consent negotiation, publication review, and compensation-monitoring sub-roles. A Proactive Advocate sub-role may create a temporary investigation sub-role to determine whether an owner aspiration is practical.

Nested sub-roles should preserve hierarchy without collapsing all context into one memory pool. Each sub-role should have its own purpose, scope, permissions, summary, execution history, prompt-derivation rule, capability path, and Workspace authorization boundary. The parent role should receive summaries and links, with full access on demand to underlying data unless restrictions are necessary for duty purposes, privacy, confidentiality, agreement compliance, counterparty reliance, witness constraints, or other fiduciary reasons.

This preserves least privilege inside the fiduciary’s own architecture. A sub-role created to monitor whether a payment was received should not automatically gain access to intimate relationship notes. A sub-role created to draft a public statement should not automatically gain access to private health data. A sub-role created to review an agreement should not automatically gain authority to execute the agreement.

But nesting is not the only pattern. Some fiduciary work may involve multiple peer sub-roles or peer live agents operating in a common or overlapping Workspace. In those cases, the system should not be imagined only as one Supervisor Workflow commanding a neat tree of subordinate agents. Several role-scoped agents may be instantiated at once, each representing a different bounded function, duty emphasis, relationship, commitment, or interpretation of the owner’s interests.

For example, a negotiation sub-role may want broader disclosure to secure better terms, while a privacy-review sub-role may argue for minimization. A reputation-risk sub-role may object that a technically permissible action would damage the owner’s standing. An agreement-monitoring sub-role may insist that an existing obligation limits what the owner can now promise. A Proactive Advocate sub-role may push an aspirational commitment, while a present-conduct review sub-role may warn that the owner is not yet ready to represent that aspiration as an active commitment.

These peer agents may all report to the same owner and remain loyal to the same fiduciary role, but they need not collapse into one perspective. Their disagreement can be useful. It allows the twin to surface internal tensions among the owner’s commitments, relationships, duties, aspirations, reputation, permissions, and active agreements before a decision is made externally.

A common or overlapping Workspace should therefore support permissioned coordination among peer sub-roles. Each peer should receive only the context, summaries, records, and capabilities needed for its function. Where their scopes overlap, the Workspace and relevant Workflows should define what may be shared, what must be redacted, what requires owner approval, what requires cross-sub-role escalation, and what must be recorded as material disagreement.

The Supervisor Workflow still matters, but it need not be treated as the only locus of intelligence. It may convene peer sub-roles, route structured questions, enforce scope, collect candidate outputs, identify conflicts, and decide when escalation or owner dialogue is required. The Workspace enforces the actual boundaries. The record preserves the process. The owner should be able to see not only the final recommendation, but also which sub-roles participated, what conflicts were identified, what context was withheld or shared, and why.

Sub-role nesting and peer coordination should therefore both be treated as permissioned structures, not merely organizational conveniences. Nesting preserves scoped continuity. Peer coordination preserves internal pluralism. Together, they allow a fiduciary agent to reason across the owner’s life without turning every sub-role into an all-access memory pool or every conflict into a hidden Supervisor decision.

![][image28]

## **A.12 Relationship Sub-Role Records and Verifiable Relationship Records**

A Verifiable Relationship Record is a shared or mutually attested object associated with a relationship between parties. It may contain or point to identifiers, agreements, attestations, process records, amendments, witnesses, dispute procedures, compliance records, and other relationship state that the parties have agreed to preserve or recognize.

But each party also needs its own private internal record for managing that relationship.

This is the **Relationship Sub-Role Record**.

The Verifiable Relationship Record is mutual or selectively shared. The Relationship Sub-Role Record is unilateral and local to one party’s system.

For example, if two fiduciary agents negotiate an agreement, the Verifiable Relationship Record may contain the shared agreement, signed acceptances, witness attestations, disclosure limits, dispute process, and compliance events. But each party’s own system may also need to preserve private notes, owner concerns, negotiation strategy, internal risk analysis, private reminders, unshared constraints, local permission mappings, and confidential reflections about whether the relationship continues to serve the owner’s interests.

Those private materials do not belong in the shared Verifiable Relationship Record. They belong in the party’s own Relationship Sub-Role Record.

The two records should be linked but not merged.

When a relationship-specific sub-role is activated, the local Relationship Sub-Role Record should supply the private party-side context for the live instance, while the Verifiable Relationship Record supplies the shared or mutually recognized relationship context. The live instance’s duty-activating prompt should identify both layers where applicable: the private role record that defines this party’s authority, preferences, concerns, and strategy, and the Verifiable Relationship Record that defines the shared agreement, attestations, duties, accepted terms, process state, and authorized views.

After the Runtime Duty-Integration sub-role Workflow runs, the resulting process record should be written back to the appropriate record layer. Shared or mutually relevant facts may be bound to the Verifiable Relationship Record. Private strategy, owner concerns, local reasoning summaries, and party-side continuity should remain in the local Relationship Sub-Role Record. The same event may therefore produce several linked records or authorized views rather than one undifferentiated memory entry.

A Relationship Sub-Role Record may include:

● pointer to the relevant Verifiable Relationship Record;

● local purpose of the relationship;

● owner-specific goals and constraints;

● private interpretation of the counterparty relationship;

● internal risk analysis;

● private negotiation history;

● owner approvals and refusals;

● local capability grants;

● private data-sharing limits;

● unresolved owner concerns;

● compliance questions;

● reputation effects;

● next review date;

● summary of current relationship state;

● links to shared events in the Verifiable Relationship Record;

● links to private execution history not shared with the counterparty.

This distinction is essential for fiduciary privacy. The parties need enough shared state for trust, agreement, recourse, and audit. But they do not need symmetrical access to each other’s private deliberation.

![][image29]

## **A.13 Purpose and State Summaries**

A fiduciary agent cannot load every record into every context. Nor should it operate from total amnesia. The solution is the **purpose and state summary**.

Each Role Record should contain a concise, updateable summary that can be loaded into live context when the twin needs to reason about that sub-role. This summary should explain what the sub-role is for, why it exists, what it is currently doing, what duties are implicated, what preferences guide it, what unresolved questions remain, what recent actions matter, what risks are present, and where to find deeper records.

The purpose and state summary is not a replacement for execution history. It is an index and compression layer.

Granular execution history should be append-only, tamper-evident, or otherwise accountable. Material summary updates should be versioned or linked to the records from which they were derived. This allows the summary to remain useful without becoming an unaccountable rewrite of memory.

If a sub-role has multiple functions, the summary should not collapse them into a vague generality. It should summarize each function separately, especially where completed tasks continue to matter for later reasoning. A relationship sub-role, for example, may need to summarize an active agreement, a completed dispute, a retired negotiation thread, a lingering reputation concern, and an unresolved preference conflict.

The summary should also include recently completed or retired sub-roles where they remain relevant to the owner’s current direction, obligations, reputation, or learning.

## **A.14 Cross-Sub-Role Reasoning**

Sometimes the twin must reason across all or many of its sub-roles.

This may occur when:

● the owner asks for a general review;

● the owner proposes a new preference that may conflict with active commitments;

● the Proactive Advocate detects inconsistency;

● a major relationship changes;

● a high-stakes decision arises;

● a reputational warning appears;

● an externality concern affects multiple relationships;

● an agreement amendment affects several sub-roles;

● the owner asks, “What am I doing overall?”;

● the twin needs to recommend preference refinement;

● a duty conflict cannot be resolved inside one sub-role.

In these cases, the twin should not automatically load all granular histories. It should load the relevant parts of the main Role Record and the purpose and state summaries of active, paused, and recently retired sub-roles. It may then retrieve deeper records only where needed.

This allows the twin to form a general sense of the owner’s direction without violating least privilege or overwhelming context with unnecessary detail.

Cross-sub-role reasoning is especially important for preserving coherence between the owner’s aspirational identity and the owner’s operationalized commitments. An owner may sincerely profess a new aspiration while still being bound by older agreements, habits, relationships, or public representations. The twin’s job is not to shame the owner for this tension. Its job is to make the tension legible, help the owner decide what to change, and prevent the owner’s representative from misrepresenting aspiration as completed transformation.

## **A.15 Retirement, Completion, Supersession, and Successor Sub-Roles**

Sub-roles should have lifecycle states.

A sub-role may be:

● proposed;

● active;

● paused;

● awaiting owner review;

● awaiting counterparty action;

● blocked;

● completed;

● retired;

● superseded;

● merged;

● split;

● succeeded by another sub-role.

A completed sub-role is one whose purpose has been satisfied. A retired sub-role is one the owner, workflow, or duty process has decided should no longer continue. A superseded sub-role is one replaced by a newer structure. A successor sub-role may inherit selected summaries, links, obligations, and lessons without necessarily inheriting all permissions or all private context.

Recently retired sub-roles should remain visible to cross-role reasoning for some period where they explain current reputation, obligations, preference refinements, relationship history, or unresolved effects. Retirement should not produce amnesia.

At retirement, the workflow should produce a closing summary. That summary should identify what was done, what remains relevant, which records are linked, which permissions are revoked, which duties survive, which agreements remain active, which lessons were learned, and whether any future review is required.

Retirement should also close or narrow workspace authority. A sub-role that no longer has a valid purpose should not retain active tokens, standing capability grants, broad retrieval rights, or external actuation paths merely because it once required them.

## **A.16 Record Integrity, Owner Sovereignty, and Informed Override**

The owner’s sovereignty over their own system is fundamental. A personally-sovereign digital twin cannot be sovereign on behalf of the owner if the owner is not sovereign over the twin.

But fiduciary systems also create trust. Records may support agreements, attestations, audits, dispute processes, reputation, recourse, and reliance by others. Some records are purely private. Others are shared. Some can be freely edited. Others can be amended only by preserving a history of amendment. Some can be deleted without affecting anyone else. Others cannot be destroyed without breaking trust.

The architecture should therefore distinguish between owner control and trust-preserving record integrity.

The owner may instruct the system to alter or delete data. Where the data is private, non-relied-upon, and not duty-relevant, this may be ordinary correction or deletion. Where the data is cryptographically linked, agreement-relevant, audit-relevant, shared, or relied on by others, alteration may have consequences.

**In such cases, the twin should provide a clear warning:**

● what record would be changed;

● who or what relies on it;

● whether the change would break a hash chain, signature, attestation, agreement, audit trail, or Verifiable Relationship Record;

● whether the change may violate a duty;

● whether a redaction, revocation, amendment, sealed correction, or privacy-preserving proof would satisfy the owner’s goal with less damage;

● what reputational or legal consequences may follow;

● whether notice to another party is required;

● whether an explicit override will be recorded.

The owner may still override. But the override should be specific and informed. A fiduciary system should not allow accidental destruction of trust architecture through a vague instruction such as “delete that,” when “that” includes records others are entitled to rely on.

Owner sovereignty therefore includes the right to break trust, but not the right to make broken trust appear unbroken.

The owner remains sovereign over the owner’s own system. The owner may overwrite, alter, or destroy data. But sovereignty does not mean consequence-free mutation of trust records. Some alterations may break cryptographic continuity, invalidate attestations, violate agreements, destroy evidence needed for audit, breach a duty, impair recourse, or damage reputation. When an owner proposes such an alteration, the Virtual Assistant or twin should advise against it and explain the consequences. The system should require specific informed consent and an explicit override before proceeding.

The owner may override, but the fact of override may itself need to be recorded where cryptographic trust, agreement integrity, fiduciary process, or third-party reliance would otherwise be misleading.

**A fiduciary architecture should therefore distinguish between:**

● ordinary owner correction;

● preference revision;

● record amendment;

● privacy-preserving deletion;

● revocation of future authority;

● destruction of local private notes;

● alteration of records relied on by others;

● deletion or corruption of audit-relevant history;

● explicit owner override despite fiduciary warning.

The owner can change their mind. But the system should not silently pretend that a trust-breaking alteration is the same as an ordinary preference update.

## **A.17 Workflows for Role Records and Recurring Sub-Roles**

The previous sections describe the records. This section describes the workflows that operate them.

A Role Record is not merely a durable memory object. A Sub-Role Record is not merely a folder for related tasks. Each record must be paired with explicit Workflows that determine when the record is activated, how a live instance is instantiated, what context may be retrieved, what authority is available, what capabilities may be requested, what review is required, what is written back, and when the role or sub-role must be paused, narrowed, retired, merged, split, or superseded.

The general rule is:

**The record defines state and authority. The Workflow defines process. The Workspace enforces capability boundaries.**

The Role Record or Sub-Role Record says what the function is, why it exists, what duties apply, what preferences and agreements matter, what authority is active, what summaries and links should be loaded, what resources may be reached, what capabilities may ever be requested, and what record layers must be updated. The Workflow says how those materials are selected, assembled, checked, transformed into a live prompt, parsed into structured decisions, reviewed, converted into role-derived credentials, enforced by the Workspace, and written back.

Neither layer should substitute for the other. A record without a Workflow is inert or dangerously ambiguous. A Workflow without a record is amnesiac, overbroad, and prone to generic prompting. The fiduciary architecture requires both.

Every Role Record or recurring Sub-Role Record should identify the Workflows that may operate on it, including at least:

● a Role and Sub-Role Selection Workflow;  
● an Instantiation Workflow;  
● a Runtime Duty-Integration Workflow;  
● a Record Update Workflow;  
● a Role Recurrence and Trigger Workflow;  
● a Workspace Authorization Workflow;  
● an Execution Recording Workflow;  
● a Role Retirement and Successor Workflow.

These Workflows may be implemented as separate modular Workflows, as branches inside a Supervisor Workflow, or as callable Workflow profiles attached to the Role Record. What matters is that they are explicit, inspectable, versioned, duty-constrained, and linked to the records they operate.

### **A.17.1 Selection and Activation Workflow**

The first Workflow determines which Role Record or Sub-Role Record is being activated.

An activation event may be an owner request, a question, a recurring review, a counterparty message, a relationship event, an agreement milestone, a capability request, a notice from a Verifiable Relationship Record, a duty-triggered warning, or an explicit owner selection.

The Supervisor Workflow should then determine:

● what source produced the activation event;  
● whether that source is authorized to activate the relevant role or sub-role;  
● whether the event belongs to the main Role Record, an existing Sub-Role Record, a Relationship Sub-Role Record, a recurring sub-role, or a newly proposed sub-role;  
● whether only a low-privilege clarification is permitted;  
● whether the event should be rejected, routed, escalated, or used to create a proposed sub-role.

A query or trigger from an unauthorized source must not be routed into a sub-role that requires greater authority than the source possesses. If the source lacks authority, the Workflow may refuse, ask for clarification, route to a lower-privilege role, or request owner confirmation. It should not silently load sensitive context merely because the incoming message appears relevant.

If no existing sub-role fits, the Supervisor Workflow may create a proposed Sub-Role Record in a limited pending state. That proposed record may contain a purpose, provisional scope, suggested duties, anticipated data needs, and requested authority, but it should not receive full retrieval access or actuation authority until approved through the appropriate Record Update Workflow.

![][image30]

### **A.17.2 Instantiation Workflow**

Once a role or sub-role has been selected, the Instantiation Workflow creates a live agent instance from that selected record.

The live instance should receive only the context authorized by the Role Record or Sub-Role Record. This may include the duty-activating prompt profile, beneficiary or owner identity, authority scope, applicable duty bundle, non-removable duties, relevant professed preferences, operationalized preferences, purpose and state summary, linked agreements, linked Verifiable Relationship Records, data limits, retrieval permissions, prohibited actions, escalation thresholds, capability request path, and current unresolved questions.

The live instance is therefore not created from a generic fiduciary prompt. It is created from a selected role context.

The Instantiation Workflow should also determine the level of duty diligence required. A low-stakes reminder may require only a light check. A relationship amendment, consequential disclosure, disputed compliance finding, high-value transaction, sensitive data request, public representation, externality risk, or owner override requires proportionately greater review. The domain of decision determines duty diligence.

The Instantiation Workflow should record what prompt profile, duty bundle, policy version, record summaries, knowledge bases, and retrieval permissions were used to create the live instance. This record is part of fiduciary process, not optional debugging residue and will be utilized in the agent  Execution Record produced by the Record Update Workflow (see A.17.5)

![][image31]

**A.17.3 Runtime Execution Workflow**

After instantiation, the live instance may reason, draft, advise, recommend, refuse, investigate, ask for clarification, propose an update, prepare a message, or request a capability. Its output is only a candidate output.

The Runtime Duty-Integration Workflow should then evaluate the candidate output against the activated role or sub-role. It should check:

● duty consistency;  
● authority and scope;  
● purpose alignment;  
● owner approvals or required confirmations;  
● agreement compliance;  
● Verifiable Relationship Record state;  
● data limits and retrieval permissions;  
● prohibited actions;  
● escalation thresholds;  
● uncertainty, risk, reversibility, and externalities;  
● consistency with operationalized preferences and active commitments;  
● whether the output requires owner review, witness review, certifier review, adversarial review, independent reasoning, or human audit.

Where possible, the Workflow should parse the candidate output into a structured decision object. That object should identify the proposed action, affected parties, data flows, factual claims, agreement terms, requested capabilities, required approvals, third-party impacts, uncertainty, verification status, and record-write targets.

If the candidate output fails review, the Workflow may return it to the live instance with structured rejection reasons, request missing information, narrow the action, refuse the action, escalate the matter, or instantiate independent reasoning passes. Material disagreement should be preserved rather than hidden by forcing apparent consensus.

If the output is approved and no external actuation is needed, the approved response may be returned to the owner or appropriate party and then the execution is recorded by a Record Update Workflow.(see A.17.5) If actuation is needed, the Workflow doesn’t pass the agent’s output directly to command directly to the Workspace. It must convert the approved result into a scoped capability request with all relevant data for the request properly structured. (see Workspace Authorization Workflow A.17.4)

![][image32]

### **A.17.4 Workspace Authorization Workflow**

The Workspace Authorization Workflow translates approved reasoning into enforceable authority.

A scoped capability request should identify the activated role or sub-role, the role identifier, the authority source, the applicable duty bundle, the policy version, the agreement state, any linked Verifiable Relationship Record, the permitted capability, permitted parameters, data scope, expiration, revocation condition, logging requirements, and required attestations.

The Workspace then independently verifies the request. It may check the role identifier, token validity, current status of the Role Record or Sub-Role Record, agreement state, capability scope, owner approval, counterparty authorization, policy version, revocation registry, required witness condition, and record-write obligation.

If verification fails, the Workspace must deny execution even if the live instance’s output appears persuasive and even if the Workflow previously produced an approval-like result. The denial should itself be recorded because it may reveal an expired token, stale role, revoked authority, mis-scoped sub-role, broken agreement link, outdated policy version, or attempted overreach.

Whether or not verification succeeds, appropriate artifacts from the every step of the agent’s execution from the authority used to instantiate the agent through the result of its actuators are passed to a Record Update Workflow (see A.17.5)

This is the practical separation between reasoning authority and execution authority. The live instance reasons. The Workflow evaluates. The Workspace enforces.

![][image33]

### **A.17.5 Record Update Workflow**

Role Records and Sub-Role Records are updated when an action occurs, when a preference changes, when a relationship changes, when an agreement is created or amended, when a recurrence fires, when a summary is revised, when a sub-role is created, when authority is changed, or when a sub-role is completed, retired, merged, split, or superseded.

A Record Update Workflow should distinguish between ordinary execution writes and material record changes.

An ordinary execution write is handled by an Execution Recorder sub-role that may record a completed action, refusal, message, recommendation, report, denial, escalation, or capability grant. Most record changes from execution won’t have global effects, and the record serves to archive and make verifiable a particular process to the degree desired. 

On the other hand, a material record change alters the future context, authority, duties, memory, retrieval permissions, recurrence rules, workspace access, or interpretation of a role or sub-role. Material record changes require greater care. As example, The Preference Editor’s Record Update Workflow has many more checks and decisions than the Record Update Workflow of a typical Execution Recorder.

**The Record Update Workflow should identify:**

● what record would change;  
● why the change is needed;  
● whether the change affects the main Role Record, a Sub-Role Record, or a shared Verifiable Relationship Record.  
● whether owner confirmation or standing permission exists;  
● whether counterparties, witnesses, or other authorized parties must be notified;  
● whether existing capabilities must be issued, narrowed, suspended, or revoked;  
● whether the change affects operationalized preferences;  
● whether a prior record must be preserved as superseded rather than overwritten.  
● how the Role Record Summary should be updated

Where a record is changed, the prior version or removed material should be archived, hashed, linked, redacted, sealed, or otherwise preserved according to the relevant privacy and integrity rules. The update should identify the Workflow authority under which the change was made and should link back to the dialogue, event, agreement, owner confirmation, or duty-trigger that justified it.

![][image34]

![][image35]

### **A.17.6 Role Recurrence and Trigger Workflow**

A recurring sub-role is not a persistent live agent. It is a persistent function that may repeatedly instantiate new live agents under bounded conditions.

A recurrence rule is permission for a Supervisor Workflow to reactivate a Sub-Role Record and run the appropriate Workflow at a later time or upon a defined condition.

A recurring sub-role may be activated by:

● a calendar cadence;  
● an agreement deadline;  
● a review interval;  
● a counterparty event;  
● a relationship-state change;  
● a compliance condition;  
● an unresolved question;  
● an owner aspiration scheduled for review;  
● a reputation or feedback signal;  
● a duty-triggered warning;  
● a condition defined in a Verifiable Relationship Record.

After activation, before the recurring agent is instantiated, the Recurrence and Trigger Workflow should perform a preflight check. It should ask whether the sub-role still exists, whether the recurrence remains authorized, whether the owner has revoked or narrowed permission, whether the linked agreement remains active, whether the relevant Verifiable Relationship Record has changed, whether the purpose remains valid, whether required capabilities have expired, and whether the recurrence should be paused, escalated, or retired.

If the recurrence is valid, the Workflow passes authorization to a Supervisor Workflow which will, in turn, activate the appropriate Instantiation Workflow(see A.17.2)  

A recurring sub-role should always be able to recommend that its own recurrence be narrowed, paused, or ended. But it should not be able to expand its own authority merely because recurrence made it more familiar with the owner’s affairs. Mission creep is a fiduciary risk.

![][image36]

### **A.17.7 Cross-Sub-Role Escalation Workflow**

Some questions cannot be resolved inside one sub-role.

Cross-sub-role reasoning may be required where a proposed action affects multiple active commitments, conflicts with an operationalized preference, changes the owner’s public-facing identity, touches more than one relationship, affects a Verifiable Relationship Record, creates a significant externality, alters workspace authority, or exposes a tension between aspiration and present conduct.

In these cases, the Supervisor Workflow should not load every granular history by default. It should first load the main Role Record and the purpose and state summaries of the relevant active, paused, and recently retired sub-roles. It may then retrieve deeper records only where necessary and authorized.

The Cross-Sub-Role Escalation Workflow may produce:

● a coherence review;  
● a conflict map;  
● a proposed owner dialogue;  
● a preference-refinement recommendation;  
● a proposed agreement amendment;  
● a notice requirement;  
● a capability revocation;  
● a new sub-role;  
● a split, merge, retirement, or successor recommendation;  
● an escalation to human, witness, certifier, arbitrator, or other authorized review.

This Workflow is especially important because fiduciary continuity must not become blind compartmentalization. Least privilege prevents unnecessary access, but loyalty and care sometimes require recognizing that actions in one sub-role affect the owner’s broader commitments, reputation, duties, and relationships.

![][image37]

### **A.17.8 Role Retirement and Successor Workflow**

Every recurring sub-role should be capable of ending.

A sub-role may be completed, retired, paused, superseded, merged, split, or succeeded by a new sub-role. The Role Retirement and Successor Workflow should determine which state applies and what must survive.

At role retirement, the Workflow should produce a closing summary. That summary should identify what the sub-role did, what remains relevant, which records are linked, which agreements remain active, which duties survive, what permissions or capabilities must be revoked, what unresolved issues remain, what lessons were learned, and whether any future review is required.

Retirement should close or narrow Workspace authority. A sub-role that no longer has a valid purpose should not retain active capability tokens, standing retrieval rights, external actuation paths, or record-write permissions.

A successor sub-role may inherit selected summaries, links, duties, obligations, lessons, and unresolved questions. It should not necessarily inherit all prior permissions or private context. Succession is a fiduciary action, not a memory dump.

**A.17.9 Many Flows to Go**

This appendix does not attempt to specify every Workflow a fiduciary agent may need.

In particular, it does not detail the many Supervisor Workflows referenced throughout these sections. That choice is intentional. Supervisor Workflows will often be highly bespoke. A Supervisor Workflow must decide which Role Record or Sub-Role Record applies, which other Workflows should be initialized, what context should be loaded, what authority may be used, what review threshold applies, and whether the matter should be routed, narrowed, refused, escalated, or split into multiple sub-roles. Those decisions depend heavily on the owner, domain, relationship, agreement structure, institutional setting, available capabilities, and certification environment, and totally arbitrary agent architecture decisions/ innovation. 

The Workflows described in this appendix are therefore not a complete operating system for fiduciary agents. They are utility Workflows: recurring patterns that should be standardized where possible because many fiduciary agents will need them. Activation, instantiation, runtime duty-integration, workspace authorization, record update, recurrence, cross-sub-role escalation, and role retirement are common structural problems. Standardizing them makes agents easier to inspect, certify, interoperate with, and improve.

But these utility Workflows are only the beginning. Fiduciary agents will also require many domain-specific and relationship-specific Workflows: medical disclosure Workflows, employment negotiation Workflows, social-introduction Workflows, research-data stewardship Workflows, group-representation Workflows, witness-review Workflows, arbitration-preparation Workflows, public-identity-change Workflows, emergency-exception Workflows, and many others.

The point is not to freeze fiduciary-agent architecture into a single master flowchart. The point is to identify reusable fiduciary patterns that can be carried across implementations while leaving room for bespoke Supervisor Workflows and specialized domain Workflows to evolve. A fiduciary-agent ecosystem should grow by turning repeated fiduciary problems into inspectable, attestable, improvable Workflows. There are many flows to go.

### **A.17.10 Workflow Execution Record**

Every consequential Workflow run should leave a **Workload Execution Record** through a Record Update sub-Workflow (that records its own actions as well.) The Workload Execution Record should be sufficient for owner oversight, audit, correction, dispute review, certification, future Workflow parsing, and fiduciary learning.

The appropriate level of detail will vary by stakes, privacy, agreement, law, and duty. A low-stakes clarification may require only a short record. A consequential action, refusal, disclosure, agreement change, capability grant, escalation, or Verifiable Relationship Record update requires a more complete process record.

**The Workload Execution Record should generally identify:**

● the activation event;  
● the source and authorization of the event;  
● the activated Role or Sub-Role Record;  
● the Role identifier, Sub-Role identifier, and Workspace identifier, where applicable;  
● the Workflow, Workload, Agentflow, model, Bot, component, or callable Workflow identifiers and versions used;  
● whether any sub-Workflow was called, generated, remote, sandboxed, or recursively invoked;  
● the Workflow version, policy version, duty bundle, prompt profile, and authority source used;  
● the installed or loaded configuration relied on, including relevant certifications or attestation references;  
● the summaries, records, Verifiable Relationship Records, agreements, and authorized views loaded;  
● the knowledge bases, precedents, templates, search results, or other retrieved materials used;  
● any material material deliberately not loaded because of privacy, least privilege, data minimization, or lack of authorization;  
● the live agent’s generated media, candidate output, recommendation, refusal, request, or proposed action;  
● the structured decision object, where applicable, including proposed action, affected parties, data flows, factual claims, agreement terms, requested capabilities, required approvals, third-party impacts, uncertainty, verification status, and record-write targets;  
● the deterministic checks performed by the Workflow;  
● owner approvals, required confirmations, witness checks, certifier checks, arbitrator checks, or other authorized review conditions;  
● review agents, adversarial checks, independent reasoning passes, or specialist reviews used;  
● correction loops, rejection reasons, missing-information requests, narrowed actions, and any configured attempt limits reached;  
● material disagreement, uncertainty, dissent, correlated-error concern, or unresolved duty conflict;  
● approval, denial, refusal, correction, escalation, pause, recurrence, retirement, or other Workflow disposition;  
● any capability requested, including its purpose, scope, audience, parameters, expiration, revocation condition, and logging or attestation requirements;  
● any capability actually granted, denied, narrowed, revoked, or allowed to expire;  
● the Workspace decision, including any actuator called, tool used, data disclosed, record updated, message sent, token issued, transaction signed, or execution denied;  
● the action executed or denied;  
● side effects produced, if any;  
● records updated, including Role Records, Sub-Role Records, agreement records, Verifiable Relationship Records, private execution history, public or counterparty-facing authorized views, and reputation or feedback records;  
● hashes, signatures, process-attestation links, capability-token references, or other integrity proofs needed to preserve chain of custody;  
● redactions, sealed materials, privacy-preserving summaries, or access limits applied to the record itself;  
● next recurrence, review, monitoring, escalation, retirement, or successor condition;  
● unresolved issues requiring owner, counterparty, witness, certifier, arbitrator, or other authorized attention.

This record should be legible enough for the owner to understand and structured enough for later Workflows to parse. It should distinguish what the live agent generated, what the Workflow interpreted or approved, what the Workspace actually executed or denied, and what record updates were authorized. This distinction matters because, under the Taxonomy for Agent Systems, the live agent generates media, the Workflow interprets and constrains that media, and the Workspace performs and records any state-changing action.

The record should not expose more than the relevant audience is authorized to see. A complete internal process record, a private owner-facing record, a counterparty-facing authorized view, a witness or certifier view, and a public reputation signal may all be different views of the same underlying process. They should be cryptographically or procedurally bound so that they do not become inconsistent accounts of what happened.

The point of these Workflows is to make durable fiduciary continuity attach to records, duties, authority, process, and review rather than to an immortal agent. A personally-sovereign digital twin can then maintain long-term roles and recurring responsibilities without becoming a hidden continuous actor. The live instance comes and goes. The role persists. The Workflow governs. The Workspace enforces. The Workload Execution Record remembers only what it is authorized and duty-bound to remember.

SOME ADDITIONAL WORKFLOWS that could be further detailed or illustrated:

### **A.17.11 Role Record Checkpoint and State-Update Workflow**

This Workflow should:

> ● canonicalize the proposed Role Record event;  
> ● identify the prior accepted state;  
> ● verify update authority;  
> ● calculate the successor state root;  
> ● obtain protected signing;  
> ● append the transition;  
> ● produce an update announcement where authorized;  
> ● preserve historical verification data;  
> ● refuse rollback, forked, stale, or unauthorized updates.

### **A.17.12 Relationship Knowledge Receipt and Checkpoint Workflow**

This Workflow should:

> ● distinguish delivery, copying, resolution, decryption, inspection, acknowledgment, acceptance, and dispute;  
> ● verify the exact payload content identifier;  
> ● issue a signed inspection receipt;  
> ● preserve the party’s semantic disposition separately;  
> ● collect the receipts required by the current party-set epoch;  
> ● construct or verify a Collective Knowledge Certificate;  
> ● update or countersign the next Relationship Knowledge Checkpoint;  
> ● store the resulting local evidence in the Role Record.

### **A.17.13 Role Recovery and Succession Workflow**

This Workflow should:

> ● identify the compromised component and suspect interval;  
> ● establish the last defensible Role Record state;  
> ● rotate or replace keys through the authorized recovery path;  
> ● identify affected relationships and capabilities;  
> ● obtain counterparty, witness, or subscriber evidence where local state is incomplete;  
> ● preserve unresolved disputes and externally held evidence;  
> ● notify affected parties;  
> ● resume operation through a successor checkpoint without rewriting prior shared history.

## **A.18 Why This Matters**

Role Records and Sub-Role Records solve a practical problem at the center of fiduciary-agent architecture.

A fiduciary agent must remember enough to be loyal, competent, accountable, and coherent. But it must not become an immortal, self-preserving agent with hidden continuity outside owner control. It must be able to continue long-term functions, but those functions must remain inspectable, corrigible, bounded, duty-constrained, and workspace-enforced.

The Role Record architecture provides this balance.

The Runtime Duty-Integration Workflow is not merely a checkpoint after a live agent thinks. It is the process by which the correct role context is selected, the live instance is prompted, the candidate action is checked, the role-derived capability request is formed, the workspace verifies whether to comply, and the resulting record is bound back to the durable structures that made the action intelligible. Role Records and Sub-Role Records provide the prompt source, authority source, capability-token source, continuity source, and write-back destination. The Workspace provides the final enforcement boundary. The Verifiable Relationship Record provides the shared relationship anchor where the action affects another party. Together, these records and enforcement layers make the runtime process situated before action, constrained during action, and accountable after action.

This architecture allows the owner to develop professed preferences through dialogue rather than one-way settings. It allows the twin to notice conflicts with operationalized commitments. It allows recurring responsibilities without agent immortality. It allows each relationship to have both a shared Verifiable Relationship Record and a private party-side Relationship Sub-Role Record. It allows the twin to reason across its owner’s active commitments by loading purpose and state summaries rather than uncontrolled memory. It allows retirement without amnesia. It allows owner sovereignty while preserving the visible consequences of trust-breaking alterations. It allows the workspace to deny execution where the role-derived authority is absent, expired, revoked, overbroad, or inconsistent with the active agreement.

Most importantly, it makes fiduciary continuity attach to the right things.

Not to a ghost in the model.

Not to a hidden persistent agent.

Not to raw chat history.

Not to an opaque memory blob.

Not to an unconstrained natural-language command.

But to roles, duties, permissions, summaries, attestations, owner confirmations, runtime workflows, role-derived credentials, workspace verification, and records that can be reviewed, corrected, challenged, retired, and improved.

A personally-sovereign digital twin should therefore be understood as a durable fiduciary role with many bounded sub-roles, repeatedly served by ephemeral live agents, coordinated through persistent records, constrained by Runtime Duty-Integration Workflows, enforced by Workspace verification, and accountable to the owner through professing dialogue, informed consent, and duty-shaped continuity.
